My interpretation of motorcycles is that they are much cheaper to buy, maintain, fuel, store and insure than cars, with the downside being that they can be more dangerous to operate in certain driving situations.

Since I am not exactly well established financially and my student loans can only be forgiven through death, I am very much attracted to getting a motorcycle over a car.

-

I have already done some research online, such as the required licensing/gear, avoiding sport bikes for lower insurance rates, getting a cheap bike for practice first before getting a more luxurious one, and so on. I just have some more questions I am hoping could be clarified on;

-

-How can I best minimize my insurance rate?

-Any student discounts I can take advantage of?

-What company should I buy from? Harley, Honda, Yamaha etc?

-What type of bike should I buy? Sport, Standard, Tourer, etc?

-Is there anything I should know as a motorcyclist, such as etiquette, expectations, warnings?
Because of financial reasons, I am considering a motorcycle to be my new main form of transport, when the public metro, a regular bicycle, and my own two feet just doesn't cut it.

I have multiple motorcycles, and use them as my main mode of transportation. Here are some tips:

Do you live in a location where there is lot of rain/inclement weather?
If it's just rain, get a decent dual sport. (should run you around $3000 for something reliable) If its lots of snow, you're probs better off with a shitty little truck.

If its nice and sunny most of the year, I would suggest a cheap but speedy standarish/sport bike with upright seating (Bandit 600, SV650, Fz1)

That will cover the basis of "what should I get" for your location.

Almost all bikes are going to be cheaper to insure than a car.

As for what company you should look for, look for any UJM (Universal Japanese Motorcycle) from 98 and newer.
In my experience, Harleys break down A LOT and Italian bikes are tempermental and expensive to repair.

I know it kinda contradicts what I just said about UJMs, but if you're a new rider, a cheap dual sport (Older Husqvarna, or an XR600, DRZ400, KLR650, DR650) is going to be your best bet on both price and forgivingness to a new rider. You want something that you're not gonna feel bad about dropping, and all of those bikes will get right back up and ask for more if you lay them down, and all of them except the DRZ400 will eat up highway miles without much fuss or discomfort (Your hands may get a little tired from the thumper engine vibrating if you do more than 90 mins on the freeway though.)

As for etiquette, expectations and warnings:

Be nice on the road and don't ride like a hooligan unless you've got some experience, and ride like every car/truck/suv is out to kill you no matter what, drop your speed by 10% if its raining and stay in higher gears than normal for your speed (less torque means less wheel spin means less chance of losing traction).

Tl;dr: Do it, you won't regret it.
Where do you recommend I get the gear and the actual motorcycle? Should I buy it from a dealer, or trust that I can buy it used off of ebay or something?

For gear, you're gonna wanna try on anything you buy (for the first time). I would recommend your local Cyclegear store.

As for getting the bike, me personally, I always use craigslist, but thats because I know what to look for in a bike (Chain/sprocket wear, fork seals, tires, and most importantly judging the shit out of the current owner.)

If you don't know what to look for, have the seller meet you at a local bike shop, they should look at it for you for free, and if not might charge you anywhere from $20-$50 to have a mechanic inspect it for you.

I can't comment on the prices in the U.S. But I would suggest a Japanese brand.

They are reliable and "cheap" to maintain.
I'm thinking of picking up that $4,200 Honda Rebel.

That's a nice bike!

However, I do agree with /u/Flat4Life that a motorcycle is not necessarily the cheapest option. I strongly suggest you invest in safety gear, but each to their own I guess.

Here are some pointers: http://www.clarity.net/adam/buying-bike.html

Personally, the first thing I look at when buying a bike are the chain and sprockets. They usually tell you the story. They aren't as easily replaced as tires and show you how the bike has been treated. (cleaned, not too loose, no kinks, no sprocket teeth missing/wear)

Good luck with whatever you'll do!
